title: CD8 PET Imaging Before and After Stereotactic Radiation Therapy for Oligoprogressive Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer
official: Tracking Radiation-Activated CD8 Engagement (TRACE): A Pilot Study of CD8 PET Imaging to Monitor Immune Activation in Oligoprogressive Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer Treated With Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
summary:
This pilot study is testing whether a new PET/CT imaging scan can show changes in immune cells after stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. The scan uses investigational imaging agents that attach to CD8-positive T cells. CD8-positive T cells are immune cells that can help the body recognize and fight cancer.

Participants with 1 to 5 growing bone metastases will receive standard SBRT to a selected bone metastasis. They will have a CD8 PET/CT scan and blood draw before SBRT and shortly after completing SBRT. The study will compare the CD8 PET signal in the treated tumor before and after radiation and will also examine untreated tumors.

The main question is whether SBRT increases the CD8 PET signal in the treated bone metastasis, suggesting that radiation may increase immune-cell activity within the tumor. The study also will assess whether the imaging procedure is safe and feasible and explore whether changes in the scan are related to blood-based immune markers and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Male adults age 18 years or older.
* Diagnosis of metastatic castration-resistant prostate adenocarcinoma.
* One to five progressing bone metastases that can be treated with stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT).
* At least one bone metastasis that is suitable for SBRT and measures at least 1.5 cm in its longest dimension.
* At least one additional bone or lymph node metastasis that will not be treated with SBRT for comparison on imaging.
* Testosterone level of 50 ng/dL or lower, or currently receiving anti-androgen therapy.
* Receiving a stable prostate cancer treatment regimen of androgen-deprivation therapy, alone or with one androgen receptor pathway inhibitor, for at least 12 weeks before the first research PET scan. No change in this treatment regimen may be planned before completion of the second research PET scan.
* Prostate-specific antigen level of at least 0.2 ng/mL.
* ECOG performance status of 0, 1, or 2.
* Adequate blood counts, kidney function, liver function, albumin, and alkaline phosphatase levels.
* Able to complete SBRT, study drug administration, and two PET/CT scans.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Cancer spread to the liver, lungs, brain, or other internal organs.
* Small-cell, neuroendocrine, or other aggressive-variant prostate cancer.
* Prior radiation to the planned treatment site when additional radiation would exceed safe limits for nearby normal tissues.
* A change in androgen-deprivation therapy or androgen receptor pathway inhibitor treatment within 12 weeks before the first research PET scan, or a planned change before the second scan.
* Recent or current treatment with chemotherapy, PARP inhibitors, radiopharmaceutical therapy, immunotherapy, cancer vaccines, systemic corticosteroids at or above prednisone-equivalent 10 mg/day, or other systemic immune-suppressing medicines. Required washout is 4 weeks or 5 drug half-lives, whichever is longer.
* Bone metastasis causing high-grade spinal cord compression, spinal instability, or an impending fracture requiring urgent surgery or standard palliative treatment.
* Active second cancer, except basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer.
* Active autoimmune or inflammatory disease that could affect immune-cell imaging results.
* Active, uncontrolled infection.
* Uncontrolled or symptomatic HIV, hepatitis B, or hepatitis C.
* Serious uncontrolled heart conditions, such as left ventricular ejection fraction below 40%, unstable arrhythmia, or unstable angina.
* Known allergy or hypersensitivity to GEH200520, \[18F\]GEH200521, or any component of the imaging agents.
* Medical, psychiatric, or logistical condition that, in the investigator's judgment, would make study participation unsafe or prevent completion of study procedures.
